speaker: Doctor
text: I am Dr. Agent. I understand you are experiencing sudden-onset vertigo; to help me diagnose the cause, please describe exactly when this started and if you have any hearing loss or ringing in your ears. Also, have you experienced any trouble speaking, double vision, or weakness in your limbs?

speaker: Patient
text: 59-year-old male. The patient presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset sensation that the room is spinning, leading to several episodes of nausea and vomiting. The symptoms started as he was going to bed and lasted for approximately 3 minutes. He mentions that he has never experienced anything like this before and currently feels at his baseline.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the details. Since your symptoms lasted only about three minutes and you have returned to baseline, are you a smoker with any history of heart disease, high blood pressure, or diabetes? Additionally, did you notice any numbness, weakness, or difficulty swallowing during those few minutes?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Sudden-onset sensation of the room spinning. I also have Nausea, Vomiting, Dizziness.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for confirming. To further differentiate between a stroke and an inner ear issue, please tell me if you have a history of high blood pressure, diabetes, or smoking, and did you experience any numbness or weakness in your face, arms, or legs during that episode? REQUEST TEST: MRI_Brain with diffusion-weighted imaging. REQUEST IMAGES: MRI_Brain.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV).

The patient's history of brief (3-minute) spontaneous episodes resolving completely, combined with normal vital signs and a lack of focal neurological deficits, strongly supports a diagnosis of BPPV rather than a stroke or vestibular neuritis.
